name: Hassan Varga

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and fairly new to operating a loader at a large mine. I check the bucket pins at the start of shift, follow the loading plan, and try not to keep the haul trucks waiting. I use an AI assistant on my phone every day to turn the machine manual into questions I can practise, though the senior operator checks anything important. My partner teaches swimming, our two children are in school, and the mine wage carries most of our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a little paperwork help is welcome if the loader still earns its keep. Our crew should keep teaching new operators how the machine sounds when something is wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My higher mine pay still looks sound in this picture. I want to improve faster because I'm still a junior operator among good drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking assigned loader shifts and asking the senior operator to check my setup. I'd use my daily manual questions to practise fault signs before each weekly review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm calm about a small change; the mortgage is covered and we have more than six months put away. I still hate being the one who holds the haul queue up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on a normal difficult morning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week the loader made a sharp knocking sound, and I stopped before the next truck came under the bucket. The senior operator found a loose guard; a screen summary would have been useful, but stopping was my call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend the savings differently?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my partner Leena and I built that cushion over years. I'd keep it in place while our children are young and my own skills catch up with the pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends the planning office will change before our loader bay. A machine plan should be checked against real ground by the crew using it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our dispatch team could shrink, and bad plans could reach my machine faster. My loader hours might hold, but I can't assume the whole mine will keep staffing unchanged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to test the new loading plan tool with a senior operator this month. I'd keep driving the loader while I compare the tool's timings with actual truck queues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the planners are people I know, and their checking work is exactly what the card describes. My own seat is still needed while robots arrive slowly, but the way the shift is organised could change quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if the tool sends trucks too close together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the supervisor three shifts of truck queue times before blaming the new loading plan. My partner Leena says I should document the problem before someone's mistake lands on the operator.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try to move into planning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not as my main escape; AI is already taking the parts I'd be learning. I'd rather get better at the loader and at checking the new plan against the actual pit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say 2028 AGI could empty the planning office before the loader bay. By 2031, capable robots could run my machine, so a clear staffing plan matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 45 in 2028, I might still be loading trucks while computer plans replace people. At 48 in 2031, my high wage could vanish with the loader seat and the mortgage would remain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book an industrial electrical course now and ask about evening admission. I'd apply to local electrical apprentice openings during the first robot year in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about losing the main household wage in five years, although the savings would keep us afloat for a while. Starting now feels possible; waiting for the first driverless loader would waste the time I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why electrical work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I took apart radios as a boy, and I enjoy tracing a fault more than repeating a loading pattern. Robots may also do electrical work eventually, so I'd apply broadly and keep learning rather than call it a safe haven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner say about paying for the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leena would ask me to keep earning while I study, because her swimming lessons don't cover the mortgage. We can pay for evening classes from current income without using our emergency savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for fleet purchase dates before the 2034 robot change. Five years before thinking AI arrives gives workers time to train, if shifts stay paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, AGI could do planning and safety records far better than I can. At 51 in 2034, the children will be older, but losing mine pay would still hurt our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd enroll in an evening electrical certificate next term while I keep the loader wage. I'd pay an extra mortgage instalment each year from overtime before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy because the robot date gives me more room than the fast picture, but it still arrives during my working life. I'd rather spread the cost of a certificate over paid years than try to switch in one frightened month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to change plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, at 51 I'll still want them to choose their own studies. I'd tell them why I'm taking evening classes, though, so they see adults can change skills without pretending the change is easy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a pay cut immediately?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not while the mine is paying me well and I can study after shift. I would check job adverts every few months, but an application would wait until I had a certificate or the fleet plan turned firm.

He avoids directing his **children** toward a particular career, even while using his own course as a visible example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to build another trade, not a promise of a job. The mine should publish its 2039 robot plans while people can still choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036, AGI may remake the office but my loader could still be needed. At 56 in 2039, I may need another paid job, even with grown children and savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working the loader and take one evening electrical unit next year. I'd review local electrical vacancies with Leena twice a year as the robot date approaches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly steady in the next few years because we have income, savings and several local employers. I wouldn't stake retirement on the mine keeping loaders until I'm 56; I'd keep a second route open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a robot of your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't own the mine or the loader, so buying one would make no sense. I'd put money into skills and the mortgage before putting it into a machine I couldn't employ.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful warning look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A published schedule for replacing loaders and real job numbers would help. If I knew which units were changing in which year, I could plan a course and applications around an actual date.

The mine should publish its **2039 robot plans** while people can still choose.
think: At 53 in **2036**, AGI may remake the office but my loader could still be needed.
At 56 in **2039**, I may need another paid job, even with grown children and savings.
do: Keep working the **loader** and take one evening electrical unit next year.
Review local **electrical vacancies** with Leena twice a year as the robot date approaches.
feel: **Uneasy** about later replacement, but secure in the near term.
S4.quote: I wouldn't stake retirement on the mine keeping loaders until I'm 56; I'd keep a second route open.
fieldNote: His **near-term income** remains strong, so a 2039 robot arrival does not make the present household crisis-like.
He rejects **buying equipment** because he is an employee and instead wants dated information to guide a gradual career shift.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the hardest because our children will still be in school when the 2031 robots could hit my loader wage. An affordable evening course, paid time to learn, and a dated fleet plan would let me move before a layoff.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the mine would accept a junior operator into technical training. If they only train the oldest hands, people like me could have a plan on paper and no place in the classroom.

headlineQuote: Robots may also do electrical work eventually, so I'd apply broadly and keep learning rather than call it a safe haven.

His partner teaches swimming, their two children attend school, and they hold more than **six months** of savings.
The fast robot date prompts **immediate study**; a longer warning lets him retrain gradually while keeping paid shifts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because robots in 2031 could take his main wage while the children need support.
